## About this course

**Authors:** Prof Anne O'Connell, Dr Isabel Olegário, Dr Rona Leith

**Affiliation:** Dublin Dental University Hospital, Trinity College Dublin

This course was developed as part of the research study *"Novel learning strategies for undergraduate dental education: the effectiveness of an online self-paced course and the impact of gamification features in learning outcomes in Dental Traumatology"*.

The course has 11 lessons: a baseline quiz, Terminology, the Dental Trauma Index, Examination and Special Tests, Trauma Splint, Uncomplicated Crown Fractures, Complicated Crown Fractures, Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, course feedback and a final quiz. Lessons are meant to be taken in order.

Some images and videos in this course are used with permission from the Dental Trauma Guide website.

slides.title: Dental Traumatology — Terminology
slides.body:
**Learning Outcomes:**

To be knowledgeable in the correct terminology describing:
- Soft tissue injuries
- Hard tissue injuries
- Injuries of supporting structures

slides.title: Procedures
slides.body:
*Glossary of Terms*

*American Association of Endodontics 2020*

items.heading: Splint
items.body: An apparatus used to support, protect or immobilise teeth that have been loosened, replanted/repositioned, fractured or subjected to certain endodontic surgical procedures.

items.heading: First-stage root canal treatment
items.body: Removal of the necrotic tissue/non-vital pulp and temporary dressing of the canal - usually with calcium hydroxide.

items.heading: Partial Pulpotomy
items.body:
- Also known as Cvek pulpotomy
- The removal of a small portion of the vital coronal pulp as a means of preserving the remaining coronal and radicular pulp tissues.

items.heading: Crown-lengthening
items.body: A surgical procedure designed to increase the extent of supragingival tooth structure for restorative or esthetic purposes by apically positioning the gingival margin, removing supporting bone, or both

items.heading: Autotransplantation
items.body: The transplantation of teeth from one site to another in the same individual, involving the transfer of embedded, impacted or erupted teeth into extraction sites or into surgically prepared sockets.

items.heading: Decoronation
items.body: The crown of the tooth is removed to 2mm below the crestal bone, and the ankylosed root is left in the alveolus to be substituted by bone.

slides.title: APEX - Glossary of Terms
slides.body: *American Association of Endodontics 2020*

items.heading: Foramen (Foramina)
Radiographic apex
items.body:
- The tip or end of the root as determined radiographically
- Its location can vary from the anatomic apex due to root morphology and distortion of the radiographic image

items.heading: Apex locator
items.body:
- An electronic instrument used to assist in determining the root canal working length or perforation
- Operates on the principles of resistance, frequency or impedance.

items.heading: Apexification
items.body: A method to induce a calcified barrier in a root with an open apex or the continued apical development of an incompletely formed root in teeth with necrotic pulps.

items.heading: Apexogenesis
items.body:
- A vital pulp therapy procedure performed to encourage continued physiological development and formation of the root end;
- Frequently used to describe vital pulp therapy performed to encourage the continuation of this process

items.heading: Regenerative Endodontics
items.body: Treatment aiming at ingrowth of new vital tissue after removal of necrotic pulp in teeth with immature root development.

slides.title: Soft Tissue Injuries
slides.body:
Abrasion, Contusion, Laceration and Avulsion.

The classification is the same for intra oral and extra oral soft tissue injuries.

items.heading: Abrasion
items.body: A superficial wound produced by rubbing or scraping of the skin or mucosa leaving a raw, bleeding surface.

images.alt: Abrasion of the skin around the nose and upper lip

items.heading: Contusion
items.body: A bruise without a break in the skin or mucosa. Subcutaneous or submucosal haemorrhage in the tissue. A contusion may be isolated to the soft tissue but may also indicate an underlying bone fracture.

images.alt: Contusion of the upper gingiva

items.heading: Laceration
items.body: A shallow or deep wound penetrating into the soft tissue, usually produced by a sharp object. May disrupt blood vessels, nerves, muscles and involve salivary glands. Most frequently seen in lips, oral mucosa and gingiva.

images.alt: Lacerations of the lower lip mucosa

slides.title: Hard Tissue Injuries
slides.body:
Enamel fracture, enamel-dentine fracture, enamel-dentine-pulp fracture, root fracture, crown-root fracture and alveolar fracture.

There are no differences in the terminology for primary and permanent dentitions.

items.heading: Enamel Fracture
items.body: A fracture confined to the enamel with loss of tooth structure. This image illustrates an enamel fracture on tooth 11 (upper right central permanent incisor).

images.alt: Enamel fracture of tooth 11

items.heading: Enamel-dentine fracture
items.body: A fracture confined to enamel and dentin with loss of tooth structure. This image illustrates an enamel-dentine fracture on tooth 21 (upper left central permanent incisor). Note that there is no visible pulp exposure - this should be evaluated carefully clinically.

images.alt: Enamel-dentine fracture of tooth 21, red arrow

items.heading: Enamel-dentine-pulp fracture
items.body:
A fracture involving enamel and dentin with loss of tooth structure and exposure of the pulp.

This image illustrates an enamel-dentine-pulp fracture on tooth 21 (upper left central permanent incisor). Note that there is a clear clinical pulp exposure.

images.alt: Two views of an enamel-dentine-pulp fracture of tooth 21, red arrow

items.heading: Root fracture
items.body:
A fracture involving dentin, cementum and the pulp. This can happen at any level of the root.

This periapical radiograph shows a root fracture on tooth 11 (middle third of the root). Note a radiolucent line indicated by an arrow.

images.alt: Periapical radiograph with a root fracture of tooth 11, white arrow

items.heading: Crown-root fracture
items.body:
A fracture involving enamel, dentin and cementum. It may or may not expose the pulp.

This image illustrates a crown-root fracture on tooth 11 (upper right central incisor).

Note that the fracture line extends into the root (arrow) and the coronal fragment has been avulsed.

images.alt: Two views of a crown-root fracture of tooth 11, red arrow

items.heading: Alveolar fracture
items.body:
A fracture of the alveolar process. This image illustrates an alveolar fracture (red arrows indicate fracture line).

Note avulsion of tooth 11 and lateral luxation of tooth 12.

images.alt: Alveolar fracture with avulsed 11 and luxated 12, yellow arrow

slides.title: Luxation injuries
slides.body:
Concussion, subluxation, extrusive luxation, lateral luxation, intrusive luxation and avulsion.

There are no differences in the terminology for primary and permanent dentitions.

items.heading: Concussion
items.body: An injury to the tooth-supporting structures without abnormal loosening or displacement of the tooth, but with marked pain to percussion.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of concussion

items.heading: Subluxation
items.body: An injury to the tooth-supporting structures resulting in increased mobility, but without displacement of the tooth.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of subluxation

items.heading: Extrusive luxation
items.body: Partial displacement of the tooth out of its socket.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of extrusive luxation

items.heading: Lateral luxation
items.body: Displacement of the tooth in a direction other than axially. Displacement is accompanied by comminution or fracture of either the labial or the palatal/lingual alveolar bone.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of lateral luxation

items.heading: Intrusive luxation
items.body: Displacement of the tooth into the alveolar bone. This injury is accompanied by comminution or fracture of the alveolar socket.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of intrusive luxation

items.heading: Avulsion
items.body: The tooth is completely displaced out of its socket.

images.alt: Dental Trauma Guide illustration of avulsion

slides.title: External Inflammatory Root Resorption
slides.body:
**Definition:**
- The combination of bacteria in the root canal (pulp necrosis) **AND** cemental/PDL damage (luxation injuries) on the external root surface results in external inflammatory root resorption.

**Clinical signs:**
- The pulp is necrotic
- Negative sensibility tests

**Radiographic signs:**
- Radiolucent areas along the root

{{img:0}}

Case: Both upper incisors were avulsed with prolonged extra-oral time (>10h). Note external inflammatory root resorption is present in the right periapical radiograph (3 months after).

**Internal Inflammatory Root Resorption**
- Occurs on the pulpal surfaces of the root canal as a result of bacterial infection in the root canal.
- Not usually associated with Dental Trauma.

images.alt: Two periapical radiographs of avulsed upper incisors, the right one 3 months later

slides.title: External Replacement Root Resorption
slides.body:
**Definition:**
- A pathologic loss of cementum, dentine and periodontal ligament with subsequent replacement by bone, resulting in fusion of bone and tooth.
- Also referred to as ankylosis
- Replacement resorption cannot be arrested or repaired.
- The rate of progression can vary.

**Clinical signs**
- Affected tooth presents with reduced mobility
- High percussion tone
- Tooth eruption is completely arrested
- In a growing child, infra-occlusion relative to adjacent teeth can be seen.

{{img:0}}

**Radiographic signs**
- Periodontal ligament is absent
- Direct union is seen between the alveolar bone and the root

{{img:1}}

**Long-term consequences in a growing child**
- The affected tooth will not erupt any further and result in horizontal and vertical defects of the alveolar bone.
- This defect can impact aesthetic rehabilitation in the future.
- <u>Decoronation</u> is a treatment option for patients with this condition.

{{img:2}}

images.alt: Upper central incisors with yellow and red dotted lines marking the different incisal levels
Periapical radiograph of an ankylosed upper incisor (lower edge may be cut)
Infra-occluded upper incisor in a growing child

slides.title: External Repair-Related Resorption (Surface Resorption)
slides.body:
**Definition:**
- Repair-related external resorption represents the result of the removal of injured periodontal ligament tissue next to the root surface by macrophages and osteoclasts.
- This is a self-limiting condition.
- Can occur after all types of luxation injuries but is more frequently found after lateral luxations and extrusions.

**Radiographic signs**
- It appears as a saucer-shaped cavity on the root surface mostly involving cementum.
- This cavity will be fully or partially repaired by new cementum (new Sharpey’s fibres).
- In root fractures, the surface resorption can happen near the fractured site.

**Important:**

slides.title: External Cervical Resorption
slides.body:
**Definition:**
- An invasive resorption process which usually starts in the cervical area and later spreads in a coronal and/or apical direction.
- A possible aetiology is that the cementoblast layer, for a still unknown reason, does not protect the root from osteoclastic activity.
- Dental Trauma is only one possible aetiological factor.

**Clinical signs**
- It may present as cervical cavitation, irregularity in the gingival contour and/or pinkish discolouration of the overlying enamel.
- In many cases, there are no obvious clinical signs and detection is by an incidental radiographic finding.
- It presents as a hard cavity base and periodontal probing often results in profuse bleeding.
- In advanced cases, the patient can present with pulpal and/or periapical symptoms.

**Radiographical signs**
- Variable and influenced by the size and nature of the lesion.
- Often irregular, asymmetrical radiolucency through which the root canal outline is traceable.
- Periapical radiograph allow evaluation mesial-distal plane but the third dimension (bucco-lingual plane) cannot be assessed objectively.
- CBCT can be used to aid treatment decision in certain cases and diagnose true ECR size, location, circumferential spread, proximity to root canal system and surgical planning.

images.alt: Diagram of an incisor with a cervical resorption lesion, red arrow

slides.title: Pulp canal obliteration (PCO)
slides.body:
**Definition:**
- Deposition of dentine in the pulpal surface of the root canal as a healing response to trauma.
- Not necessarily indicative of a diseased pulp.
- This is commonly observed in primary teeth.

**Clinical signs:**
- Change in colour can be seen.

**Radiographic signs:**
- Increased dentine production resulting in a calcified canal

**Case:**
- History of intrusion of the upper left central incisor (21) and corrected by orthodontic extrusion.
- Pulp canal obliteration was noted at the review appointment after 2 years.

images.alt: Two periapical radiographs of upper incisors showing pulp canal obliteration

slides.title: Apical Periodontitis
slides.body:
**Asymptomatic apical periodontitis**

Inflammation and destruction of apical periodontium that is of pulpal origin, appears as an apical radiolucent area, and does not produce clinical symptoms

**Symptomatic apical periodontitis**

Inflammation usually of the apical periodontium, producing clinical symptoms including a painful response to biting and/or percussion or palpation. It might or might not be associated with an apical radiolucent area.

slides.title: Dental Trauma Index
Eden Baysal Dental Trauma Index
slides.body:
The Eden-Baysal index is a new 5-digit index that comprises all important information and can be easily computerised.

The index contains five digits following FDI tooth code. The first two digits contain numbers starting from 0, the third digit contains capital letters, the fourth digit contains lower case first letters and the fifth digit contains plus or minus sign.

Intraoral and radiographic findings are used to record the cases with the index.

**1st digit: Crown fracture**

The 1st digit after the FDI tooth code stands for hard dental tissue injuries affecting the crown with information on its relation with the pulp and root. Intraoral clinical evaluation is used to gather information for proper coding. Numbers are used to categorise the injury in hierarchical order in relation to severity. The codes are as follows:

- 0 = none
- 1 = enamel fracture
- 2 = enamel and dentin fracture = uncomplicated crown fracture
- 3 = enamel and dentin fracture including the pulp = complicated crown fracture
- 4 = enamel-dentin-cementum fracture = uncomplicated crown-froot fracture
- 5 = Enamel-dentin-cementum fracture including the pulp

**2nd digit: Root fracture**

2nd digit stands for hard dental tissue injury of the root indicating the location of the fracture line. Numbers are used to categorise the injury in a hierarchical nature in relation to its position. The position of the fracture line in relation to the gingival margin defines the severity of the injury and impaired prognosis. In case of an oblique root fracture affecting more than one location on the root, the position of the fracture line close to the cervical region is recorded. The codes used in the second digit are as follows:

- 0 = none
- 1 = apical 1/3 root fracture
- 2 = middle 1/3 root fracture
- 3 = cervical 1/3 root fracture

**3rd digit: Luxation injury**

3rd digit stands for periodontal ligament injuries (Luxation injuries). The type of the periodontal ligament injury that is present is indicated by its first letter written in capitals. The first letters of the luxation injuries are used as follows:

- N = None
- C = Concussion
- S = Subluxation
- L = Lateral luxation
- E = Extrusive luxation
- I = Intrusive luxation
- A = Avulsion

**4th digit: Maturity and shape of apex**

4th digit stands for maturity of the apex. Radiographic evaluation reveals the characteristics of the apex in both dentitions. In an immature apex, the root has thinner dentin walls, it may be short and the apical foramen is large. In a mature apex, the apical end of the root is completely formed and the periodontal membrane has a uniform width around the root and the apex. In primary dentition, physiological root resorption may be present. Therefore, 3 codes are used in this digit. Lowercase first letters of the words defining the characteristics of the apex are used as below:

- i = immature apex
- m = mature apex
- r = resorbed apex (physiological)

**5th digit: Alveolar process fracture**

5th digit indicates the presence or absence of a fracture of the alveolar process and expressed by plus (+) or minus (-) sign, respectively. It is important to note that the fracture should be related to the alveolar process only. The definitions of the codes for this digit are as follows:

- Plus (+) sign = Alveolar process fracture
- Minus (−) sign = No alveolar fracture

**This index has been modified to include soft tissue (MEBDTI).**

**Soft tissue injury**

Soft tissue injuries affecting skin, lip and/or gingiva are recorded for each patient by adding superscript numbers outside the brackets containing the records of injured teeth and alveolar process recorded by ‘Eden Baysal Dental Trauma Index’. Multiple soft tissue injuries should be written in ascending order separated by commas as superscript numbers.

- 0 = none
- 1 = skin/lip abrasion
- 2 = skin/lip laceration
- 3 = skin/lip contusion
- 4 = skin/lip avulsion
- 5 = intra-oral abrasion
- 6 = intra-oral laceration
- 7 = intra-oral contusion
- 8 = intra-oral avulsion

slides.title: Examination and Special Tests
slides.body:
**Learning Outcomes:**

To be able to obtain a good medical, dental and dental trauma history

To be able to provide adequate extra and intra oral clinical examination, including special tests.

slides.title: Medical History
slides.body:
Obtaining a good medical history is essential to provide safe and effective management of Dental Traumatic Injuries.

Wherever possible, a comprehensive medical history should commence with information relating to pregnancy and birth, the neonatal period, and early childhood.

Previous and current problems associated with each of the major systems should be elicited through careful questioning, and here a pro forma may well be helpful.

**Systems evaluation**

- Respiratory (e.g. asthma, hayfever)
- Cardiovascular (e.g. congenital heart defects, high blood pressure, history of angina/cardiac procedures).
- Haematological (e.g. bleeding disorders, anaemia, bruising).
- Immunological (e.g. predisposition to infections, immunodeficiencies)
- Endocrine (e.g. diabetes)
- Gastrointestinal (e.g. Chron’s disease, ulcers, reflux)
- Neuromuscular (e.g. cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, neuropathies)
- Skeletal (rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, other traumatic fractures).
- Behaviour or learning problem (e.g. attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism)

**History of Hospitalisations**

This include history of previous hospitalisations (age and cause of admission, operations, previous treatments under GA).

**List of current medications**

Regular prescriptions, recent/current medication allergies (format: tablers, liquid, inhalers).

**Revelant family medical history**

Problems with GA, allergies, bleeding disorders, any sibling with significant medical history.

**History of vaccinations**

Check if the patient has been previously vaccinated against tetanus. The place of the accident may indicate a need for tetanus prophylaxis (as most teeth have been in contact with soil, or the wound itself is soil-contaminated).

slides.title: Questions related to the Injury
slides.body:
**Where did the injury occur?**

This information may have legal implications for the patient and may on occasion indicate the possibility of contamination.

**How did the injury occur?**

This may lead to identification of the impact zones.

**When did the injury occur?**

This information may be essential in relation to many injury types. In relation to a tooth avulsion the extent of time and the extraoral storage condition becomes very decisive for later treatment.

**Was the injury witnessed?**

This is especially important in children to clarify how the injury occured.

**Was there a period of unconsciousness?**

If so, for how long? Amnesia, nausea and vomiting are all signs of brain damage and require hospital referral (emergency services).

**Is there any disturbance in the bite?**

An affirmative answer may indicate a luxation injury or root fracture with displacement, an alveolar or jaw fracture or a fracture of the condylar region.

**Was any treatment provided elsewhere?**

Previous treatment (replantation, repositioning, splinting) should be considered before further treatment is provided. It is also important to ascertain how the avulsed tooth was stored (dry, milk, water).

**History of previous dental injuries**

When? Which teeth were injured? Treatment provided and by whom?

A number of patients may have experienced repeated injuries to their teeth. This can influence pulpal sensibility tests and the recuperative capacity of the pulp and/or PDL.

**Account for missing fragments**

Have you chipped or fractures any teeth? If so, where are these fragments now? Check for any soft tissue lacerations (intra and extra orally) since the fragment(s) can be embedded in soft tissue. In this case, a soft tissue radiograph will be recommended.

**Questions for avulsed teeth**

- Where were the teeth found? (dirt, asphalt,floor)
- When were the teeth found?
- Were the teeth dirty?
- When were the teeth replanted?
- Extra-oral time? Extra-oral dry time?
- Storage medium?
- Was tetanus antitoxoid given?
- Were antibiotics given?

slides.title: Clinical Examination
slides.body:
The clinician should evaluate systematically both soft and hard tissue, extra and intra-orally.

- Clean the tissues gently to remove any blood or debris to facilitate diagnosis.
- Provide good extra-oral examination and palpation of facial skeleton (check for subcutaneos haematomas)
- Evaluate temporomandibular joints (palpate directly over the joint while the patient opens and closes the mandible)
- Check for disturbances in the occlusion (e.g. step deformities)
- Evaluate extra and intra-oral soft tissues (record any soft tissue injuries, including oral mucosa, gingiva and lips).
- Exam the crowns of teeth for the presence and extent of fractures, pulp exposures or changes in colour.
- Record any displacement of teeth (luxation injuries).
- Check for abnormal mobility of teeth and alveolar process.

slides.title: Mobility Test
slides.body:
Mobility testing should determine the extent of loosening of individual teeth and mobility of groups of teeth (an indication of alveolar fracture). Mobility is best assessed using 2 blunt instruments such as mirror handles.

The degree of mobility is registered on a scale of 0 – 3 and is an aid in defining the type of luxation.

**Classification:**

0 = no loosening (physiological mobility)

1 = horizontal loosening ≤ 1 mm

2 = horizontal loosening ≥ 1 mm

3 = vertical (axial) loosening

**Important considerations:**

It is important, however, to distinguish between normal physiologic mobility and no mobility which is found in cases of intrusion and lateral luxation at the time of injury, or ankylosis in the follow-up period.

‘ 0 ‘ mobility should, therefore, be used in conjunction with percussion testing in order to distinguish between normal physiologic mobility and no mobility (see below).

slides.title: Photographic Documentation
slides.body:
The use of clinical photographs is strongly recommended for the initial documentation of the injury and for follow-up examinations.

Photographic documentation allows monitoring of soft tissue healing, assessment of tooth discoloration, the re-eruption of an intruded tooth, and the development of infra-positioning of an ankylosed tooth.

In addition, photographs provide medico-legal documentation that could be used in litigation cases.

*Reference: 2020 IADT Guidelines*

slides.title: Sensibility Testing
slides.body:
Sensibility testing refers to methods/tests utilised to <u>indirectly</u> determine pulp status (cold test and electric pulp test) by assessing <u>neural response</u> to a stimulus and not pulp vitality.

**Important considerations:**

- All pulpal stimulation is only perceived as pain and this can be inconclusive in younger children due to lack of patient cooperation/understanding of the test.
- Pulp sensibility testing is not recommended in primary teeth.
- Wait until the pain is gone before moving on to the next tooth
- The temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing, and therefore <u>is not conclusive</u> for pulp necrosis in traumatised teeth.

slides.title: Cold test
slides.body:
Stimulates hydrodynamic movement of dentinal fluid within patent dentine tubules leading to local depolarisation and generation of action potentials from intact A-delta fibres.

<u>Methods</u>

- Example of commercial product: Endo-Frost® (-50°C)
- Isolate and dry the tooth
- Apply the product using a small cotton pellet to the tooth for a maximum of 10s or until a response is felt.
- If re-testing is deemed necessary, wait for at least 1 minute to allow the tooth to recover

images.alt: Video: cold test on an upper incisor

slides.title: Electric Pulp Test (EPT)
slides.body:
Low-grade electric current stimulates intact myelinated A-delta fibres within the pulp-dental complex.

A positive response can relate to the presence of functional neurons however, it does not equate to pulpal health.

<u>Methods</u>

- The tooth needs to be lubricated with toothpaste/prophy paste to facilitate the conduction of electrical impulses
- Be familiar with your pulp tester machine (e.g. lip or hand electrode is usually needed to complete the circuit)
- The probe tip needs to be placed on an intact surface within the incisal two-thirds of the crown.
- A “tingling” sensation will be felt by the patient (positive response).
- A negative response is established after the digital display reached its maximum level, with no reaction from the patient (test it twice)

{{img:0}}

See below where the applicator tip is being placed over prophy paste for the electric pulp test of tooth 11. Note that the prophy paste should be only the placed at one tooth at a time.

{{img:1}}

images.alt: EPT probe tip on prophy paste on an upper incisor
Video: electric pulp test of tooth 11

slides.title: Limitations
slides.body:
<u>Sensibility tests</u>

- Patient anxiety
- Paediatric patients (level of understanding and behaviour)
- Contacting metal restorations
- Inadequately dried teeth: conduction of current to periodontium
- Analgesia, sedative, drugs/alcohol
- Presence of pulp canal obliteration (PCO)

slides.title: Test Cavity
slides.body:
- This method should only be used where pulp necrosis is the likely diagnosis but all other tests provided inconclusive results.
- Single tooth isolation is recommended to prevent false positive results.
- The tooth is not anesthetised and the dentist drills a small hole into the tooth (usually on the palatal surface for incisors) to reach the enamel-dentine junction.
- The patient is asked if they feel any pain during drilling. If the patient experiences pain upon contact with sound dentine, the procedure is terminated and the cavity is restored.
- If the patient does not respond, root canal treatment should be initiated (confirmed pulp necrosis).
- This test is not recommended for young children because they might not be able to distinguish pressure and pain

slides.title: Radiographic Examination
slides.body:
The clinician should evaluate each case and determine which radiographs are required for the specific case.

A clear justification for taking a radiograph is essential.

The clinician should always perform a comprehensive interpretation of the radiographic findings and report it as part of the dental trauma documentation.

items.heading: ALADAIP
items.body:
The use of ALADAIP principles (As Low As Diagnostically Achievable being Indication-oriented and Patient-specific) can help prevent unnecessary exposure as well as overexposure.

A guiding principle when considering exposing a patient to ionizing radiations (eg, either 2D or 3D radiographs) is whether the image is likely to change the management of the injury.

items.heading: Film Holder
items.body: The use of film holders is highly recommended to allow standardised and reproducible intra-oral radiographs.

items.heading: Use of different views
items.body: Radiographs are necessary to make a thorough diagnosis of dental injuries. Tooth root and bone fractures, for instance, may occur without any clinical signs or symptoms and are frequently undetected when only one radiographic view is used.

items.heading: Recommended radiographs (IADT guidelines 2020)
items.body:
Since maxillary central incisors are the most frequently affected teeth, the radiographs listed below are recommended to thoroughly examine the injured area:

1. One parallel periapical radiograph aimed through the midline to show the two maxillary central incisors.
2. One parallel periapical radiograph aimed at the maxillary right lateral incisors (should also show the right canine and central incisor).
3. One parallel periapical radiograph aimed at the maxillary left lateral incisor (should also show the left canine and central incisor).
4. One maxillary occlusal radiograph.

items.heading: CBCT
items.body:
Cone beam computerised tomography (CBCT) provides enhanced visualisation of traumatic dental injuries, particularly root fractures, crown/root fractures, and lateral luxations.

CBCT helps to determine the location, extent, and direction of a fracture. In these specific injuries, 3D imaging can be useful and should be considered, if available.

slides.title: Trauma Splint
slides.body:
**Learning outcomes:**
To be familiar with indications for splinting traumatised teeth, types of splints and recommended splinting times.

items.heading: Splinting Traumatised Teeth
items.body:
**A splint is required when teeth are mobile or need to be repositioned following a traumatic injury.**
- The aim of splinting is to stabilise the injured tooth and maintain its position throughout the splinting period, improve function and provide comfort.
- The International Association for Dental Traumatology (IADT) recommend splinting for luxated, avulsed and root-fractured teeth.
- Splinting might be also recommended for teeth with subluxation.
- Current evidence supports short-term, passive and flexible splints.
- Correct splinting is important to maximise healing of the soft and hard tissues, and prevent further injury.

items.heading: Effective splints should:
items.body:
- Be functional: it incorporates at least one uninjured tooth on either side of the traumatised tooth or teeth
- Be flexible: allow for physiological tooth movement
- Allow adequate oral hygiene
- Be comfortable for the patient
- Not irritate the soft tissues
- Allow pulp sensibility testing
- Allow endodontic access (if required)
- Not interfere with the occlusion
- Be easy to apply
- Be easy to remove without causing iatrogenic damage to the tissues

<u>Article: Tips for splinting traumatised teeth</u>

items.heading: <u>COMPOSITE AND WIRE SPLINT</u>
items.body:
Wire secured to the teeth with composite is the most favored and widely-used splint, and can be used in almost all types of tooth injury.
- The stainless steel wire should be pre-contoured to conform to the teeth and the diameter must not exceed 0.4mm or 0.016” to remain flexible.
- The wire used should be passive in nature and not exert any unwanted orthodontic forces.

images.alt: Composite and wire splint

items.heading: <u>NYLON FISHING LINE</u>
items.body: Nylon fishing line (0.13-0.25 mm) can be used to create a flexible splint, with composite to bond it to the teeth.

images.alt: Nylon fishing line splint

items.heading: <u>RESIN SPLINT (Protemp 3M ESPE)</u>
items.body:
Composite resin splints are quick to apply but can lead to gingival irritation as they can be very difficult to clean and prone to fracture.

Composite splints are rigid and therefore not recommended.

Protemp splint can be useful as a temporary emergency measure when the dentist is outside of the dental setting.

It should be replaced as soon as possible with a flexible splint.

images.alt: Resin splint (Protemp)

items.heading: <u>FIBRE SPLINT (Ribbond)</u>
items.body:
Fibre splints consist of weaved polyethylene fibres (Ribbond) or glass fibres in a polymer-resin gel matrix (EverStick).

Its advantages include high strength, easy to adapt and aesthetic.

images.alt: Fibre splint (Ribbond)

items.heading: <u>TITANIUM SPLINT</u> (Medartis).
items.body:
Titanium trauma splints are flexible titanium splints with a rhomboid mesh structure which are easily secured to teeth with a flowable composite.

Its main disadvantage is the high cost.

images.alt: Titanium splint (Medartis)

items.heading: <u>SUTURE SPLINT</u>
items.body: Suture splints may be required if there are multiple missing teeth, or in the mixed dentition where conventional splinting is not possible.

images.alt: Suture splint

slides.title: Splinting times (duration) according to IAPD Guidelines 2020

items.heading: Root fracture
items.body:
**4 WEEKS**
Stabilise the mobile coronal segment with a passive and flexible splint for 4 weeks
**UP TO 4 MONTHS**
If the fracture is located cervically, stabilisation for a longer period of time (up to 4 months) may be needed.

items.heading: Alveolar Fracture
items.body:
**4 WEEKS**
Stabilise the segment by splinting the teeth with a passive and flexible splint for 4 weeks.

items.heading: Subluxation
items.body:
**2 WEEKS**
A passive and flexible splint may be required to stabilise the tooth for up to 2 weeks in case of excessive mobility or tenderness when biting on the tooth.

items.heading: Extrusive Luxation
items.body:
**2 WEEKS**
Stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks using a passive and flexible splint.

items.heading: Lateral Luxation
items.body:
**4 WEEKS**
Stabilise the tooth for 4 weeks using a passive and flexible splint. If breakdown/fracture of the marginal bone or alveolar socket wall, additional splinting may be required

items.heading: Avulsion
items.body:
**2 WEEKS**
Stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks using a passive and flexible splint.

slides.title: What about intrusion?
slides.body:
When surgical repositioning is indicated according to the IADT guidelines, the tooth should be splinted with a passive and flexible splint for **4 weeks.**

slides.title: Enamel Infraction
slides.body: IADT Guidelines 2020

items.heading: Clinical Findings
items.body:
- No sensitivity to percussion or palpation
- Normal mobility
- Pulp sensibility tests are usually positive

**Important:** evaluate the tooth for a possible associated luxation injury or root fracture, especially if tenderness is observed.

items.heading: Radiographic findings
items.body:
- No radiographic abnormalities

**Recommended radiographs:**
- One parallel periapical radiograph
- Additional radiographs are indicated if signs or symptoms of other potential injuries are present

items.heading: Treatment
items.body:
Usually no treatment is necessary.

**Severe infractions:** sealing with flowable resin should be considered to prevent discoloration and bacterial contamination of the infractions.

items.heading: Follow-up
items.body:
- No follow-up is needed if it is certain that the tooth suffered an infraction injury only.
- If there is an <u>associated injury</u> such as a luxation injury, that injury-specific follow-up regimen prevails.

items.heading: Favourable Outcomes
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Positive response to pulp sensibility testing
- Continued root development in immature teeth

items.heading: Unfavorable outcomes
items.body:
- Symptomatic
- Pulp necrosis and infection
- Apical periodontitis
- Lack of further root development in immature teeth

slides.title: Enamel Fracture
slides.body: IADT Guidelines 2020

items.heading: Clinical Findings
items.body:
- Loss of enamel with no visible sign of exposed dentin
- Normal mobility
- Pulp sensibility tests usually positive

**Important:**
- Evaluate the tooth for any other possible traumatic dental injury, especially if tenderness is observed.
- Missing fragments should be accounted for!

items.heading: Radiographic findings
items.body:
- Enamel loss is visible

**Recommended radiographs:**
- One parallel periapical radiograph
- Additional radiographs are indicated if signs or symptoms of other potential injuries are present

**Soft tissue radiograph:**
If the fragment is missing and there are soft tissue injuries, radiographs of the lip and/or cheek are indicated to search for tooth fragments.

items.heading: Treatment
items.body:
- Polishing of tooth edges
- Tooth fragment reattachment
- Composite resin restoration

items.heading: Follow-up
items.body:
Clinical and radiographic evaluations are necessary:
- After 6-8 weeks
- After 1 year

items.heading: Favourable Outcomes
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Positive response to pulp sensibility testing
- Good quality restoration
- Continued root development in immature teeth

items.heading: Unfavorable outcomes
items.body:
- Symptomatic
- Pulp necrosis and infection
- Apical periodontitis
- Loss/failure of restoration
- Lack of further root development in immature teeth

For very small or minor enamel fractures, it can be smoothed to remove rough margins and edges. This can be performed with a polishing bur or polishing discs.

**Restoration** Depending on the patient’s behaviour and aesthetics demands, a small restoration with composite resin can be used to reestablish form and contour.

slides.body: IADT Guidelines 2020

items.heading: Clinical Findings
items.body:
- Loss of enamel and dentine tissues, with no visible pulp exposure
- Normal mobility
- Pulp sensibility tests usually positive
- No sensitivity to percussion or palpation

**Important:**
- Evaluate the tooth for any other possible traumatic dental injury, especially if tenderness is observed.
- Missing fragments should be accounted for!

items.heading: Radiographic findings
items.body:
- Enamel-dentine loss is visible

**Recommended radiographs:**
- One parallel periapical radiograph
- Additional radiographs are indicated if signs or symptoms of other potential injuries are present

**Soft tissue radiograph:**
If the fragment is missing and there are soft tissue injuries, radiographs of the lip and/or cheek are indicated to search for tooth fragments.

items.heading: Treatment
items.body:
Treatment consists primarily of protecting the pulp from external insults and restoring normal function and aesthetics. This can be achieved by:
- Tooth fragment reattachment
- Composite resin restoration
- Temporary glass ionomer restoration

items.heading: Follow-up
items.body:
Clinical and radiographic evaluations are necessary:
- After 6-8 weeks
- After 1 year

items.heading: Favourable Outcomes
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Positive response to pulp sensibility testing
- Good quality restoration
- Continued root development in immature teeth

items.heading: Unfavorable outcomes
items.body:
- Symptomatic
- Pulp necrosis and infection
- Apical periodontitis
- Loss/failure of restoration
- Lack of further root development in immature teeth

slides.title: Fragment Reattachment
slides.body:
Enamel-Dentine Fracture

**Pulp Protection**
If the exposed dentin is within 0.5 mm of the pulp, a non-setting calcium hydroxide lining can be placed.

{{img:0}}

**Fragment Reattachment**
If the tooth fragment is available and intact, it can be bonded back on to the tooth.

The fragment should be rehydrated by soaking in water or saline for 20 min before bonding

{{img:1}}

**Step-by-Step:**
- Clean the tooth and isolate the tooth area
- Etch the tooth surface with phosphoric acid 37% for 30 seconds
- Wash and dry the tooth surface
- Apply bonding agent with a microbrush on the tooth surface; air thin dry and light cure
- Apply an intermediate material (e.g. flowable resin or resin cement) on the fragment surface to be reattached
- Position the tooth fragment firmly against the tooth surface, remove any excess of the intermediate material and lightcure.

{{img:2}}

- A V- shaped external double chamfer along the junction line and a double-chamfer on the fracture line on the buccal and lingual surfaces can be used to improve aesthetics.

Fragment reattachment is the prefered option if the intact fragment is available.

images.alt: Enamel-dentine fracture of the upper left central incisor
Upper incisors after fragment reattachment
Final result of fragment reattachment

slides.title: Composite resin restoration
slides.body:
Enamel-Dentine Fracture

When the intact fragment is not available

**Pulp Protection**
If the exposed dentine is within 0.5 mm of the pulp, a calcium hydroxide lining can be placed.

{{img:0}}

**Surface Preparation**
- Rinse and dry the tooth
- Apply a thin layer of the adhesive system of choice (air-thin dry to remove any excess of the bonding system).
- Polymerisation (light cure).

{{img:1}}

- Restore the tooth with composite resin.
- Direct mock-up with composite resin can be used using a silicone index obtained from a wax-up.
- Otherwise, a free-hand composite resin restoration can be performed.
- Finishing and polishing stage with abrasive discs and diamond burs for the texture can be used to improve aesthetic results.

**Important**: In cases where fragment reattachment or composite resin restoration can not be performed, an emergency procedure that comprises the application of a temporary glass ionomer restoration is indicated to prevent bacterial invasion into the dentine tubules.

**Concomitant luxation injuries:** Restoration with composite resin restoration can be difficult to perform on teeth with increased mobility and gingival bleeding. In this case, a temporary restoration is indicated since a dry operative field is difficult to maintain.

Upper incisors after composite resin restoration

slides.title: Expected Outcomes following uncomplicated crown fractures
slides.body:
**PULP**
- The risk of pulpal complications is minimal for uncomplicated crown fractures.
- The tooth should be monitored up to 1 year after the injury - if sensibility testing is normal, no further review is needed.
- The risk of pulp necrosis is significantly increased in the case of an additional luxation injury.
- It is important to review the restoration - in case of failure, a repair/replacement of the restoration should be performed.

**PDL**
- Periodontal complications are extremely rare after crown fractures and consist only of repair-related resorption.
- The risk of PDL-related outcomes (replacement/inflammatory root resorption) is significantly increased in the case of an additional luxation injury.

slides.title: Complicated Crown Fractures
slides.body:
Enamel-dentine-pulp fracture

**Learning Outcomes:**

To be knowledgeable of complicated crown fractures, including the assessment, immediate management, long-term prognosis and treatment options.

slides.title: Enamel-Dentine-Pulp Fracture
slides.body: A fracture confined to enamel and dentin with pulp exposure.

images.alt: Illustration of an enamel-dentine-pulp fracture in an incisor

slides.title: Enamel-Dentine-Pulp Fracture
slides.body: IADT Guidelines 2020

items.heading: Clinical Findings
items.body:
- A fracture confined to enamel and dentine with pulp exposure
- Depending on the absence or presence of a concomitant luxation injury, the pulp will present with a bright red, cyanotic or ischemic appearance, respectively.
- There may be spontaneous bleeding from the pulp.
- Normal mobility
- No sensitivity to percussion or palpation
- Exposed pulp is sensitive to stimuli (eg, air, cold, sweets)

**Important:**

- Evaluate the tooth for any other possible traumatic dental injury, especially if tenderness is observed.

items.heading: Radiographic findings
items.body:
- Enamel-dentine loss is visible

**Recommended radiographs:**

- One parallel periapical radiograph
- Additional radiographs are indicated if signs or symptoms of other potential injuries are present

**Soft tissue radiograph:**

- If the fragment is missing and there are soft tissue injuries, radiographs of the lip and/or cheek are indicated to search for tooth fragments.

items.heading: Treatment
items.body:
- Partial pulpotomy (Cvek Pulpotomy) for teeth with open apices and teeth with completed root development.
- Non-setting calcium hydroxide or non-staining calcium silicate cements are suitable materials to be placed on the pulp wound.
- If a post is required for crown retention in a mature tooth with complete root formation, root canal treatment is the preferred treatment
- If the tooth fragment is available, it can be bonded back onto the tooth after rehydration and the exposed pulp is treated
- In the absence of an intact crown fragment for bonding, cover the exposed dentin with glass ionomer or use a bonding agent and composite resin

items.heading: Follow-up
items.body:
Clinical and radiographic evaluations are necessary:

- after 6-8 weels
- after 3 months
- after 6 months
- after 1 year

**Important:**

- If there is an associated luxation, root fracture or the suspicion of an associated luxation injury, the luxation follow-up regimen prevails and should be used.
- Longer follow-ups will be needed

items.heading: Favourable Outcomes
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Positive response to pulp sensibility testing
- Good quality restoration
- Continued root development in immature teeth

items.heading: Unfavorable outcomes
items.body:
- Symptomatic
- Pulp necrosis and infection
- Apical periodontitis
- Loss/failure of restoration
- Tooth discolouration
- Lack of further root development in immature teeth

slides.title: Direct pulp capping
slides.body:
**Criteria for direct pulp capping**

- Only indicated for immediate treatment of small pulpal exposures (pin point exposure)
- Direct pulp capping should be avoided in cases with delayed presentation and greater than pinpoint exposures.

**Steps of the Procedure:**

- Local anaesthesia may be required.
- The tooth should be adequately isolated
- A dressing material is placed directly over the pulp exposed area (“pinpoint exposure”)
- Non staining calcium silicate cements or calcium hydroxide should be applied to the wound and compressed slightly.

**Restoration:**

- A thin layer of glass ionomer cement can be applied over the dressing material.
- The tooth can be restored using dental adhesive with either conventional resin composite build-up or crown fragment reattachment.

**Important:**

- A temporary glass ionomer restoration can be performed in case of a lack of moisture control.

slides.title: Partial Pulpotomy
slides.body:
Also known as Cvek Pulpotomy

**Criteria for Cvek Pulpotomy**

- Partial pulpotomy can be performed up to 9 days following traumatic pulp exposure
- The outcome does not appear to be affected by exposure size if less than 4 mm
- High success rate in teeth in teeth with open apices but can also be used in teeth with closed apices.

**Steps of the Procedure:**

- Local anaesthesia and rubber dam isolation
- Remove 1–3 mm of the exposed pulp (removal of the inflamed superficial pulp tissue up to the level of a healthy pulp) using a round carbide or diamond bur (box-like cavity).
- Place a sterile cotton pellet over the pulp to achieve haemostasis (thin should occur within 5 minutes).
- If haemostasis is not achieved in 5min, a full pulpotomy is required.
- Place non-staning calcium silicate cements (such as MTA or Biodentine) or non-setting calcium hydroxide over the pulp and compress slightly.

{{img:0}}

**Restoration:**

- A thin layer of glass ionomer cement should be applied over the medicament.
- The tooth can be restored using dental adhesive with either conventional resin composite build-up or crown fragment reattachment.
- A temporary restoration with glass ionomer restoration can be performed in certain circumstances.

**Important:**

- Depending on the extent of the complicated crown fracture, evaluation by a multidisciplinary team should be considered when deciding the best restorative technique.

{{img:1}}

images.alt: Video of a partial pulpotomy procedure
Four clinical photos of the restoration steps on a fractured upper incisor

slides.title: Expected Outcomes following complicated crown fractures
slides.body:
- Partial pulpotomy and pulp capping present high success rates with respect to pulp survival.
- Radiographic evidence of hard tissue closure of the exposure can be seen 3 months after treatment.
- It is important to review the restoration - in case of failure, a repair/replacement of the restoration should be performed.
- Continued root development is expected in teeth with open apices.
- Delayed presentation (greater than 9 days) increases the chances of pulp necrosis.
- The risk of pulp necrosis is significantly increased where there is an additional luxation injury.

**PDL**

- Periodontal complications are extremely rare after complicated crown fractures and consist only of repair-related resorption.
- The risk of PDL-related outcomes (replacement/inflammatory root resorption) is significantly increased where there is an additional luxation injury.

slides.title: Case-based Learning
slides.body:
A 10-year old boy fell from his bike. He attended for treatment 30 hours after the incident. There was no relevant medical history.

In this case, apart from a complete trauma history, it is important to <u>locate</u> the missing fragment.

Always check for any intra and extra-oral lacerations (in case it is embedded in the soft tissues) or any breathing difficulties (aspiration).

If the fragment is found, it can be used for fragment reattachment. In this case, the fragment could not be located.

**Clinical presentation:**

{{img:0}}

Note that a complicated crown fracture is present on tooth 21 (enamel-dentine-pulp fracture). The pulp is clearly exposed. It is important to check for increased mobility or displacement to diagnose any additional luxation injury (impact on prognosis).

The exposed pulp can sensitive to stimuli (eg, air, cold, sweets)

**Radiographic Assessment:**

One parallel periapical radiograph was taken. Observe that no root fractures was noted and the apex is not completely closed yet. Note that the fracture line is above the bone level.

{{img:1}}

**Emergency Treatment:**

In patients where teeth have immature roots and open apices, it is very important to preserve the pulp. Partial pulpotomy was performed in order to promote further root development.

In this case, non-staining calcium silicate cement (CSC) was applied over the pulp.

{{img:2}}

Resin-modified glass ionomer cement (RMGIC) was placed over the CSC and the tooth was then restored with composite resin.

{{img:3}}

slides.title: Avulsion of Permanent teeth
Avulsion of Permanent Teeth

images.alt: Illustration of avulsion: empty socket and the tooth displaced out of it
Video showing a tooth being knocked out of its socket

items.heading: Visual signs
items.body: The tooth is removed from its socket.

items.heading: Percussion test
items.body: Not indicated.

items.heading: Mobility test
items.body: Not indicated

items.heading: Sensibility test
items.body: Not indicated

items.heading: AT THE PLACE OF ACCIDENT
items.body:
1) Keep the patient calm

2) Find the tooth and pick it up by the crown (the white part) - avoid touching the root

3) If the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or in the patient’s saliva and encourage the patient/parent to replant the tooth in the original position in the jaw.

4) Bite on a tissue to hold the replanted tooth in position.

5) Seek emergency dental treatment immediately.

items.heading: IF REPLANTATION AT THE ACCIDENT SITE IS NOT POSSIBLE
items.body:
1) Keep the patient calm

2) Instruct the patient to:

- Locate the tooth and any fragments if possible.
- Place the tooth, as soon as possible, in a storage or transport medium that is immediately available at the emergency site.

**In descending order of preference:**

**Milk > HBSS > Saliva > Saline**

*\*Although water is a poor medium, it is better than allowing the tooth dry out*

- See a dentist immediately and bring the tooth with them.

slides.title: TREATMENT GUIDELINES FOR AVULSED PERMANENT TEETH

items.heading: TREATMENT GUIDELINES FOR AVULSED PERMANENT TEETH
items.body:
The choice of treatment is related to the <u>maturity of the root</u> (open or closed apex) and the condition of the <u>periodontal ligament (PDL) cells</u>.

The condition of the PDL cells is dependent on the **time out of the mouth** and on the **storage medium** in which the avulsed tooth was kept.

{{img:0}}

**Minimizing the dry time is critical for survival of the PDL cells.**

It is critical to record information regarding:

- Extra-oral total time (EOT)
- Extra-oral dry time (EODT)
- Storage medium

images.alt: Illustration of an avulsed tooth with separation of the PDL and exposure of the root surface

slides.title: Assessing the condition of the PDL cells of an avulsed tooth

items.heading: The PDL cells are most likely viable
items.body: The tooth has been replanted immediately or within a very short time (about 15 minutes) at the place of accident.

items.heading: The PDL cells may be viable but compromised.
items.body: The tooth has been kept in a storage medium (eg, milk, HBSS (Save-a-Tooth or similar product), saliva, or saline, and the total extra-oral dry time has been <60 minutes).

items.heading: The PDL cells are likely to be non-viable.
items.body: The total extra-oral dry time has been more than 60 minutes, regardless of the tooth having been stored in a medium or not.

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines — avulsed permanent teeth with CLOSED APEX
slides.body:
If the tooth has been replanted <u>**at the site of injury or before the patient’s arrival at the dental clinic:**</u>

**1) Clean the injured area.**

- Verify the correct position of the replanted tooth both clinically and radiographically.

**2) Leave the tooth/teeth in place.**

- If the tooth is malpositioned, correct it using slight digital pressure.
- If the tooth or teeth were replanted in the wrong socket or rotated, consider repositioning the tooth/teeth into the proper location up to 48 hours after the traumatic incident.

**3) Stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks**

- Use a passive flexible splint and make sure that the area is cleansible.

**4) If there is an associated alveolar or jawbone fracture:**

- A more rigid splint is indicated and should be left in place for 4 weeks.

**5) Suture gingival lacerations, if present.**

**6) Initiate root canal treatment within 2 weeks after replantation.**

- The pulp should be removed in avulsed teeth with closed apex.
- Calcium hydroxide is recommended as an intracanal medicament for up to 1 month followed by root canal filling.

**7) Administer systemic antibiotics.**

- The use of systemic antibiotics after avulsion and replantation has been recommended to prevent infection-related reactions and to reduce the occurrence of inflammatory root resorption.
- **ADD LINK TO HSE AB**

**8) Check tetanus vaccination status.**

- If the wound contains dirt or a foreign object the patient needs to be evaluated for the need for a tetanus immunisation.

**9) Provide post-operative instructions.**

- Keep the area clean: brush teeth with a soft toothbrush after each meal.
- Use chlorhexidine (0.12% to 0.2%) mouth rinse or gel twice a day for 2 weeks.
- Maintain a soft diet for up to 2 weeks.
- Avoid participation in contact sports.

**10) Follow-up appointment in 2 weeks.**

- Review, removal of splint and initiate root canal treatment.

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines
slides.body:
If the tooth has been kept in a physiologic storage medium or stored in non-physiologic conditions, <u>**with the extra-oral dry time less than 60 minutes:**</u>

**1) Clean the tooth**

- Remove loose debris and visible contamination from the tooth by gently agitating it in the storage medium or using a stream saline.
- Keep the tooth in a storage medium during the examination and while preparing for replantation

**2) Local Anaesthesia**

- Administer local anesthesia (preferably without a vasoconstrictor) and clean the injured area

**3) Examine the alveolar socket**

- If there is a fracture of the socket wall, reposition the fractured fragment into its original position with a suitable instrument.
- Remove the coagulum with a saline stream to allow better repositioning of the tooth

**4) Replant the tooth**

- Replant the tooth slowly with slight digital pressure.
- Excessive force should not be used to replant the tooth
- Verify the correct position of the replanted tooth both clinically and radiographically.

**5) Stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks**

- Use a passive flexible splint (e.g. wire of a diameter up to 0.4 mm) bonded to the tooth and adjacent teeth. Alternatively, nylon fishing line (0.13-0.25 mm) can be used to create a flexible splint, using composite to bond it to the teeth.
- Keep the composite and bonding agents away from the gingival tissues and proximal areas.
- If there is an associated <u>alveolar or jawbone fracture</u>, a more rigid splint is indicated and should be left in place for about <u>4 weeks</u>.
- Suture gingival lacerations, if present.

**6) Root Canal Treatment**

- The pulp should be removed in avulsed teeth with closed apex.
- Initiate root canal treatment using rubber dam isolation within 2 weeks after replantation.
- Calcium hydroxide is recommended as an intracanal medicament for up to 1 month followed by root canal filling.

**7) Administer systemic antibiotics.**

- The periodontal ligament of an avulsed tooth often becomes contaminated by bacteria from the oral cavity, the storage medium, or the environment in which the avulsion occurred.
- The use of systemic antibiotics after avulsion and replantation has been recommended to prevent infection-related reactions and to decrease the occurrence of inflammatory root resorption.

**Adult and children >12 years old:**

Amoxicillin 500mg every 8h for 5 days. Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole 400mg every 8 hours for 5 days.

**Children <12 years old:**

Amoxicillin suspension (125ml/5ml or 250mg/5ml): maximum 30mg/kg per dose.

Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole suspension 200mg/5ml - maximum 7.5mg/kg per dose.

**9) Check tetanus vaccination status.**

**10) Provide post-operative instructions.**

- Keep the area clean: brush teeth with a soft toothbrush after each meal.
- Use chlorhexidine (0.12%) mouth rinse twice a day for 2 weeks.
- Maintain a soft diet for up to 2 weeks.
- Avoid participation in contact sports.

**11) Follow-up appointment in 2 weeks.**

- Review, removal of splint and initiate root canal treatment.

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines
slides.body:
<u>**Extra-oral dry time longer than 60 minutes**</u>

**CLOSED APEX (EODT>60min)**

- Follow the same protocol as described before for dry time less than 60 minutes.
- Replacement resorption will occur due to the lack of viable PDL cells.
- The decision to replant is usually the correct decision. If the tooth is replanted, the patient should be reviewed in 2 weeks for splint removal and initiation of root canal treatment.
- There are some circumstances when the replantation is not advised. For example, a delay of replantation of more than one day in an adult patient where other restorative options are available (e.g. implant, prosthesis).

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines — avulsed permanent teeth with OPEN APEX
slides.body:
If the tooth has been replanted <u>**before the patient’s arrival at the clinic:**</u>

**1) Clean the injured area with water, saline, or chlorhexidine.**

**2) Verify the correct positioning clinically and radiographically of the replanted tooth.**

- If the tooth or teeth were replanted in the wrong position, consider repositioning the tooth/teeth into the correct location for up to 48 hours after the trauma under local anaesthesia.

**3) Stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks using a flexible splint**

**4) If there is an associated alveolar or jawbone fracture:**

- A more rigid splint is indicated and should be left in place for about 4 weeks.

**5) Suture gingival lacerations, if present.**

**6) No root canal treatment is necessary at the emergency visit for avulsed teeth with open apex**

**7) Administer systemic antibiotics.**

- The use of systemic antibiotics after avulsion and replantation has been recommended to prevent infection-related reactions and to decrease the occurrence of inflammatory root resorption.
- **Adult and children >12 years old:**

Amoxicillin 500mg every 8h for 5 days. Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole 400mg every 8 hours for 5 days.

- **Children <12 years old:**

Amoxicillin suspension (125ml/5ml or 250mg/5ml): maximum 30mg/kg per dose.

Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole suspension 200mg/5ml - maximum 7.5mg/kg per dose.

**8) Check tetanus vaccination status.**

**9) Provide post-operative instructions.**

**10) Follow up.**

- Review after 2 weeks and splint removal.
- Root canal treatment should only be initiated when a diagnosis of pulp necrosis has been established (chances of revascularisation).

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines
slides.body:
If the tooth has been kept in a physiologic storage medium or stored in non-physiologic conditions, and the extra-oral time has been <u>less than 60 minutes:</u>

**1) Remove loose debris and visible contamination by agitating in the storage medium:**

**2) Keep the tooth in a storage medium during examination and while preparing for replantation**

**3) Administer local anesthesia (preferably without vasoconstrictor) and clean the area**

**4) Examine the alveolar socket**

- If there is a fracture of the socket wall, reposition the fractured fragment into its original position with a suitable instrument.
- Remove the coagulum with a saline stream to allow better repositioning of the tooth

**5) Replant the tooth**

- Replant the tooth slowly with slight digital pressure.
- Excessive force should not be used to replant the tooth back into its original position.
- Verify the correct position of the replanted tooth both clinically and radiographically.

**6) Stabilize the tooth for 2 weeks**

- If there is an associated <u>alveolar or jawbone fracture</u>, a more rigid splint is indicated and should be left in place for about <u>4 weeks</u>.
- Suture gingival lacerations, if present.

**7) Endodontic therapy is not needed at the emergency visit for avulsed teeth with an open apex with dry time less than 60 minutes**

- Pulp necrosis may not occur in these cases, therefore, the risk of external infection-related (inflammatory) root resorption should be weighed against the chances of pulp survival.

**8) Administer systemic antibiotics.**

- The use of systemic antibiotics after avulsion and replantation has been recommended to prevent infection-related reactions and to decrease the occurrence of inflammatory root resorption.
- **Adult and children >12 years old:**

Amoxicillin 500mg every 8h for 5 days. Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole 400mg every 8 hours for 5 days.

- **Children <12 years old:**

Amoxicillin suspension (125ml/5ml or 250mg/5ml): maximum 30mg/kg per dose.

Penicillin allergy: Metronidazole suspension 200mg/5ml - maximum 7.5mg/kg per dose.

**9) Check tetanus vaccination status.**

**10) Provide post-operative instructions.**

**11) Follow up after 2 weeks.**

- Review and splint removal.
- Root canal treatment should only be initiated when a diagnosis of pulp necrosis has been established (chances of revascularisation).

slides.title: Treatment Guidelines
slides.body:
**If the extra-oral time longer than 60 minutes:**

Follow the same protocols for replantation of avulsed teeth with open apex described previously.

- Pulp necrosis is almost certain in avulsed teeth with an open apex that had an extra-oral dry time longer than 60 minutes.
- First-stage root canal treatment should be commenced within 2 weeks: the pulp space needs to be cleaned to avoid inflammatory root resorption.
- Regenerative endodontic therapy can lead to further root development and can be considered instead of traditional root canal therapy.

slides.title: Delayed replantation has a poor long-term prognosis for PDL cells.

items.heading: Periodontal ligament
items.body: The periodontal ligament becomes necrotic and is not expected to regenerate.

items.heading: Expected outcome
items.body: The expected outcome is ankylosis-related (replacement) root resorption. The rate of ankylosis and resorption varies considerably and can be unpredictable.

items.heading: Goal of replantation
items.body: The goal of replantation in these cases is to restore, at least temporarily, esthetics and function while maintaining alveolar bone contour, width and height. Replantation will keep future treatment options open.

items.heading: Growing children
items.body: Parents of pediatric patients should be informed that decoronation or other procedures such as autotransplantation might be necessary later if the replanted tooth becomes ankylosed and infra-positioned, depending on the patient’s growth rate and the likelihood of eventual tooth loss.

slides.title: Delayed replantation has a poor long-term prognosis for the PULP.

items.heading: Pulp necrosis
items.body:
Pulp survival is more likely in open apex teeth with shorter extraoral time.

Pulp necrosis is very likely to occur in closed apex teeth regardless of the extra-oral time.

If spontaneous revascularization does not occur, apexification, regenerative endodontic therapy, or root canal treatment should be initiated as soon as pulp necrosis and infection are identified.

items.heading: Expected outcome
items.body:
Pulp necrosis is a common outcome for teeth following avulsion.

The timing of endodontic intervention in open apex teeth will be dictated by the likelihood of pulp necrosis and subsequent inflammatory root resorption.

Regenerative endodontic therapy can be considered in teeth with open apex to encourage continued root development.

In closed apex teeth, root canal treatment should be initiated within 2 weeks.

items.heading: Goal of replantation
items.body: Pulp survival in avulsed open apex teeth is possible and can allow continued root development. If the pulp becomes necrotic, endodontic therapy can stabilize the tooth and contribute to tooth survival.

items.heading: Growing children
items.body:
There is a potential for spontaneous healing to occur in the form of new connective tissue with a vascular supply in immature teeth with open apices.

Pulp survival is essential for continued root formation.

Regenerative endodontic therapy can be successful following trauma in open apex teeth.

slides.body:
Let’s take a look at a real-life scenario and see what would be the best approach based on the current IADT guidelines.

**EMERGENCY VISIT**

A 9-year-old child attends your practice after avulsing teeth 11 and 21. The tooth was immediately placed in milk and the accident happened only 30min ago.

When you see the teeth, you are not sure if there is a root fracture or if the teeth have open apexes.

**What should you do?**

items.body:
{{img:0}}

A radiograph can be taken before tooth replantation to evaluate the socket and the presence of tooth/bony fragments.

images.alt: Periapical radiograph of the empty sockets of teeth 11 and 21
Replanted upper central incisors with a wire splint and sutured gingival laceration

items.body:
{{img:0}}

A radiograph should be taken immediately after repositioning to verify the position of the replanted teeth.

images.alt: Periapical radiograph after replantation of teeth 11 and 21

slides.title: What's the correct answer?
slides.body: Swipe to see answers options.
slides.question: What's the correct answer?
options: Root canal treatment should be started within two weeks for the majority of avulsed teeth with open apex.
For all avulsed teeth with closed apex, root canal treatment should be started within 2 weeks after replantation.
When extraoral dry time is <60min, root canal treatment should not be started unless there are signs of pulp necrosis.
Root canal treatment is not required in a tooth with a closed apex that was replanted at the site of injury (immediately).

slides.title: STABILISATION OF REPLANTED TEETH (SPLINTING)
slides.body:
**The aim of splinting is to stabilise the injured tooth and encourage healing.**

- Current evidence supports short-term, passive and flexible splints for stabilization of replanted teeth.
- Periodontal and pulp healing are promoted if the replanted tooth is subjected to slight mobility and function.
- Replanted permanent teeth should be stabilised for a period of <u>2 WEEKS</u> depending on the length and degree of maturation of the root.
- An additional week of splinting is appropriate only if excessive trauma from the opposing dentition might further traumatise the tooth or if the avulsed tooth is unable to remain in the correct position.

{{img:0}}

<u>COMPOSITE AND WIRE SPLINT</u>

Wire secured to the teeth with composite is the most favored and widely-used splint, and can be used in almost all types of tooth injury.

- The stainless steel wire should be pre-contoured to conform to the teeth and the diameter must not exceed 0.4mm or 0.016” to remain flexible.
- The wire used should be passive in nature and not exert any unwanted orthodontic forces.
- The splint should allow adequate cleaning of the wound (hygienic).

images.alt: Composite and wire splint on the upper anterior teeth

slides.title: Trauma Review
slides.body:
Replanted teeth should be monitored clinically and radiographically.

The follow-up intervals will depend if the avulsed tooth has open or closed apex.

Review follow-up intervals in the next slide.

items.heading: Replanted teeth with closed apex
items.body:
Root canal treatment should be initiated within 2 weeks. Replanted teeth should be monitored clinically and radiographically:

- at 2 weeks (when the splint is removed)
- 4 weeks
- 3 months
- 6 months
- 1 year
- Yearly thereafter for at least five years.

items.heading: Replanted teeth with open apex
items.body:
Replanted teeth with an open apex should be monitored clinically and radiographically at :

- 2 weeks (when the splint is removed)
- 1 month
- 2 months
- 3 months
- 6 months
- One year
- Yearly thereafter for at least five years.

**NOTE:**
Avulsed teeth with open apex must be monitored actively to identify signs of pulp necrosis/inflammatory resorption.

slides.title: FAVORABLE AND UNFAVORABLE OUTCOMES
slides.body: Let’s understand the differences between the expected outcomes between avulsed teeth with closed and open apex and the influence of the extraoral dry-time in the prognosis of the case.

items.heading: Open Apex
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Functional
- Normal mobility
- No sensitivity to percussion and normal percussion sound.
- Radiographic evidence of continued root formation and tooth eruption.
- Pulp canal obliteration: this is expected and can be recognized radiographically sometime during the first year after the trauma.

items.heading: Closed Apex
items.body:
- Asymptomatic
- Functional
- Normal mobility
- No sensitivity to percussion and normal percussion sound.
- No radiolucencies and no radiographic evidence of root resorption.
- The lamina dura appears normal.

*Note that pulp treatment is always required after avulsion injuries in teeth with closed apex.

items.heading: Open Apex
items.body:
- The patient may or may not have symptoms; presence of swelling or sinus tract;
- The tooth may have excessive mobility or no mobility (ankylosis) with high-pitched percussion sound.
- Presence of radiolucencies. Radiographic evidence of infection-related (inflammatory) resorption, ankylosis-related (replacement) resorption, or absence of continued root formation.
- When ankylosis occurs in a growing patient, infra-position of the tooth is highly likely to create disturbances of alveolar and facial growth over the short, medium and long term.

items.heading: Closed Apex
Inform the patient and their family
items.body:
- Patients or parents and children need to be fully informed of the prognosis of an avulsed tooth as soon as possible.
- They should be fully engaged in the decision-making process.
- The potential costs of and time required for different treatment options should be openly discussed.

items.heading: Multidisciplinary team
items.body: - Follow-up care requires good coordination between the initial provider of treatment and specialists in secondary care services (e.g. orthodontist, paediatric dentist and/or endodontist) with the appropriate experience and training in the holistic management of complex dento-alveolar trauma.

slides.title: Treatment options
slides.body: Decision requires multidisciplinary treatment planning.

items.heading: Regenerative endodontic techniques
items.body:
RET is highly desirable especially in immature teeth to allow continued root development.

<u>Article: Clinical Perspectives of Pulp Regeneration.</u>

items.heading: MTA apexification
items.body: Apical barrier formation using MTA in immature teeth will prevent any further root development.

items.heading: Decoronation
items.body:
Decoronation is a surgical method for treating ankylosed incisors in children and adolescents.

- The crown and root filling are removed, leaving the root in situ to be resorbed and covered with a mucoperiosteal flap.
- Early loss of a permanent tooth leads to loss of alveolar bone, especially in buccopalatal width. Decoronation preserves not only the width of the ridge but also the vertical height.
- The idea is to remove the crown and maintain the resorbing root as a matrix for new bone development so the volume of the alveolar ridge can be preserved, allowing more optimal conditions for a later prosthetic solution.

<u>Article: Ridge preservation/decoronation.</u>

items.heading: Tooth loss
items.body:
The dental team should include specialists who will provide expert advice on long-term care. When tooth loss is inevitable, tooth replacement should be provided as soon as possible following extraction.

Avoidance of space loss and maintenance of alveolar ridge should be planned in growing patients.

Other treatment options can include tooth replacement by a removable space maintainer, bonded bridge, and autotransplantation, among others. Implant treatment can be considered after growth is completed.

slides.title: Case-based Learn
slides.body: Now let’s move on to a real case scenario to test your knowledge.

items.body:
A 7-year-old girl avulsed her upper right central incisor (11) while playing on the playground in school in the morning (10h15am).

The teacher found the tooth in the grass and placed it in milk (10h45).

The school contacted the child’s parents who then brought the child to the dentist. The tooth was replanted at 11h45.

**Important:**

- Extra oral time (EOT) = 1h30min
- Extra oral dry time (EODT)= 30min
- Storage medium = milk
- Tooth might be contaminated = grass

images.alt: Replanted tooth 11 with a flexible wire splint

items.body:
**When should the dentist see the child again?**

- 2 weeks for splint removal

**Should root canal treatment be initiated within 2 weeks?**

- No. The pulp status should be monitored in this situation (7 year old = open apex). Risks of developing inflammatory root resorption should be balanced against chances of pulp revascularisation. This can happen very fast, therefore the dentist should keep a close eye on the case.

**How often should the dentist see this child?**

- Replanted teeth with an open apex should be monitored clinically and radiographically at 2 weeks (when the splint is removed), 1, 2, 3, 6 months, one year, and yearly thereafter for at least five years.

**Spontaneous pulp space revascularization is possible**

- Evaluate absence of pain, fistulae or swelling
- Evaluate pulp sensibility testing: note that a false-negative response can occur after trauma
- Evaluate if the tooth is not tender to percussion - this can be normal during the first few weeks.
- Evaluate if the tooth has no increased mobility: note that depending on the stage of tooth development (e.g. short roots) this can be a normal finding
- Evaluate absence of radiographic signs of inflammatory resorption
- Evaluate absence of periapical radiolucencies - this can be difficult to see due to the large open apex of the tooth
- Evaluate if continued root development is noted radiographically - note that this can only be evaluated after 3-4 months after trauma.

{{img:0}}

After 2 months, the child attends with a buccal sinus associated with tooth 11.
